clue.text: Well-regulated trolley pusher?

blocks.note: first meaning: tidy and in good order
second meaning: a hospital attendant who wheels patients and equipment about

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the trolley pusher is a hospital porter rather than a supermarket shopper.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is an adjective for methodical, tidy conduct and also a noun for a hospital attendant doing routine tasks.

clue.text: A few of the foregoing with this alternative

blocks.note: the clue before this one is number 1
the word that offers an alternative
this clue is number 2

explanation.surface: A puzzling instruction to pick a handful of earlier items or this new option instead.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue numbers themselves are the wordplay: the previous clue is 1 down and this one is 2 down, so the answer reads 'one or two'.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a casual way of saying a small number, just a couple of things.

clue.text: Both the dials go wrong: this you must see!

indicators.note: letters that go wrong fall out of their proper arrangement and must be put right

blocks.note: letters taken as written for the anagram

explanation.surface: Both clock faces have broken down, and the result is apparently a spectacle worth witnessing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go wrong' reads as one phrase, but GO belongs to the letters to be shuffled and only 'wrong' signals the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: A sight to behold is something remarkable, a spectacle that anyone ought to look at.

clue.text: ... This suffice, or do you want the usual saloon?

indicators.note: the question asks whether we want those two short words in another arrangement

blocks.note: this clue is number 4
taken as written for the anagram

explanation.surface: Following 'one or two', a car salesman asks whether this will do or whether a standard saloon is wanted.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis continues 2 down: one or two, or will four suffice? As at 2 down, the clue's own number supplies a word.
explanation.definitionFit: A saloon, the British word for a sedan car, normally has two doors on each side, four in total.

clue.text: Keeper of the watch, an unknown copper, coming in: he's earthborn

indicators.note: the unknown and the copper come in and settle inside the watch keeper

blocks.note: a fob is the chain or pocket that holds a pocket watch
X is the classic unknown quantity in algebra
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: A watchman, a mystery policeman and some newcomer described as being of humble earthly birth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' looks like a policeman but is the metal; 'earthborn' is literal, since a fox's den is called an earth.
explanation.definitionFit: Young foxes are born underground in a den known as an earth, so a young one is literally earthborn.

clue.text: It's made of batter clumsily ground

definitions.note: a verb: to land an aircraft flat and heavily

blocks.note: first meaning: a flat cake fried from batter
second meaning: to bring an aircraft down flat and hard

explanation.surface: Something bashed about by a cricketer at the crease, then pounded roughly to powder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Batter' and 'ground' suggest cricket or milling; in fact ground is to bring down to the ground, as a pilot does.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a flat fried food and, as a verb, describes an aircraft dropping flat onto the runway in a heavy landing.

clue.text: Report of pachyderms in pass with peculiar feature

indicators.note: a report is what is heard, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: rhinoceroses are thick-skinned pachyderms
a confirming hint: split in two, the pass's name describes a crooked facial feature

explanation.surface: Somebody hears of big beasts spotted in a mountain pass, and notes a strange characteristic.
explanation.walkthrough: Wrynose Pass is a steep road in England's Lake District; split into two words, the name describes a crooked nose.
explanation.definitionFit: Wrynose is the name of a well-known mountain pass in Cumbria, a route over the fells.

clue.text: From river to river back to river

indicators.note: going back means this river's name is read from its end

blocks.note: the Po is the great river of northern Italy
taken as written
the Cam is the river through Cambridge

explanation.surface: A traveller hopping from one waterway to another and then returning, a whole tour of rivers.
explanation.walkthrough: The word river appears three times; the last one is the definition, an American river flowing past Washington DC.
explanation.definitionFit: The Potomac is the river on which Washington DC stands, flowing into Chesapeake Bay.

clue.text: The birds are over the pond (saying in parts of the Dodecanese

definitions.text: The birds are over the pond

indicators.note: only some of the island group's name is used, its opening part dropped
the saying sits inside the remaining letters

blocks.note: the Greek island group's name without its first four letters
an adage is a proverb or saying

explanation.surface: Birds migrate across the sea, with a proverb heard in the Greek islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over the pond' is slang for across the Atlantic, in North America; the missing closing bracket is in the original clue.
explanation.definitionFit: These large grey-brown waterfowl are native to North America, which is across the Atlantic from Britain.

clue.text: Having got my ape movies muddled, I say I'm king of the river

blocks.clueFragment: Having got my ape movies muddled, I say
blocks.note: the speaker blends two ape films, Tarzan's 'Me Tarzan' and King Kong
Tarzan-style speech puts me where I am belongs
in the muddle, King is swapped for its partner word from the film title King Kong

explanation.surface: Someone confused by jungle films declares themself monarch of a waterway.
explanation.walkthrough: The muddle mixes 'Me Tarzan' with King Kong, so 'I'm king' comes out as ME KONG.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mekong is the great river of Southeast Asia, running from Tibet through Laos, Cambodia and Vietnam.

clue.text: On All Fools' Day the bird gets old fruit

blocks.note: April Fools' Day is 1 April, written APR I
a cock is a male bird

explanation.surface: On 1 April a bird gets its hands on some stale fruit, perhaps as a prank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old fruit' sounds like a jovial British form of address but asks for an archaic fruit name.
explanation.definitionFit: Apricock is the early English name for the apricot, used by Shakespeare and his contemporaries.

clue.text: Accommodation like 6

blocks.note: first meaning: an apartment on one floor
second meaning: as level as the batter-made item at 6 down

explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points at 6 down; 'flat as a pancake' is the stock phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is the British term for an apartment and also an adjective for something level and thin.

clue.text: The president finds something explosive in "The King and I"  ...

indicators.note: the explosive sits inside the letters of the musical's title

blocks.note: The as written, K for king, and I as written, with and simply joining them
a bomb is something that explodes

explanation.surface: A head of state discovers a bomb planted in a production of the Rodgers and Hammerstein musical.
explanation.walkthrough: The bomb goes in after TH, splitting THE. He became president of South Africa in 1999, the year of this puzzle, the first of a linked chain of clues.
explanation.definitionFit: Thabo Mbeki succeeded Nelson Mandela as president of South Africa, serving from 1999 to 2008.

clue.text: ... in his place - enough to give one a fit - a chorus ...

indicators.note: giving the following words a fit throws them into convulsions and out of their order

blocks.note: taken as written for the anagram
taken as written for the anagram

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: the president at home, with a singing group loud enough to cause a seizure.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipses chain this clue to 13 across, so 'his' is the president there.
explanation.definitionFit: Thabo Mbeki was president of South Africa, so that country is the place belonging to him.

clue.text: See 3
Pet on a table set to change and not to change

definitions.text: set to change and not to change

indicators.note: the table word is set up to change one of its letters

blocks.note: a cat is a household pet
taken as written
a table is a list, with its I changed to Y

explanation.surface: A cat sitting on a laid table, about to cause havoc yet staying calm itself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' puts the pet first in a down answer; the definition is the paradox of an agent that causes change but stays unchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: In chemistry, a catalyst speeds up a reaction while remaining chemically unaltered itself at the end.

clue.text: Roman bridge (of the kite?) takes motorway left by way of the north

blocks.note: the M1, Britain's first motorway
L is the standard abbreviation for left
via means by way of
N is the abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: A Roman bridge, perhaps named after a bird of prey, with a road route going north.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the motorway from London to Yorkshire. The bracketed kite hint refers to Latin milvus, kite, which the bridge's name echoes.
explanation.definitionFit: The Milvian Bridge crosses the Tiber in Rome, scene of Constantine's famous victory in 312 AD.

clue.text: Collusion with accountant is a big laugh

blocks.note: CA is a chartered accountant
a hoot is a burst of laughter
is shortened to 's

explanation.surface: An accountant caught conspiring with clients turns out to be great fun.
explanation.walkthrough: The verb is is contracted to 's and goes after the laugh, not before it.
explanation.definitionFit: To be in cahoots is to be in secret partnership, the usual idiom for scheming collusion.

clue.text: ... at last the  balladist admits his identity (Guardian article by a neighbour)

blocks.note: Z is the last letter, as in A to Z
W S Gilbert signed his Bab Ballads as Bab, so admitting it he says I'm Bab
the newspaper's editorial voice speaks as we
the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Continuing the chain, a ballad writer finally owns up, in a newspaper piece about someone next door.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At last' feels like 'finally' but is the last letter of the alphabet. A Zimbabwean is a neighbour of South Africa from the previous clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Zimbabwe shares a border with South Africa, so a person from there is a neighbour.

clue.text: What the sheep said about punishment under the Gaekwar

definitions.note: names the state the Gaekwar ruled

indicators.note: the bleat goes around the punishment, enclosing it

blocks.note: the bleat of a sheep
the rod is a traditional beating

explanation.surface: A sheep bleats about a beating handed down under an Indian ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: The Gaekwar was the title of the maharaja who ruled the princely state in western India.
explanation.definitionFit: Baroda, now Vadodara, was the princely state ruled by the Gaekwar dynasty in Gujarat.

clue.text: Poles in their customary order in a French city

indicators.note: the poles hold the next part between them, one at each end

blocks.note: north and south, the two poles
north is usually placed before south, and ante is Latin for before

explanation.surface: Polish people lined up in their usual sequence in a city in France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' suggests people from Poland but means the north and south poles; N ante S is Latin for 'N before S'.
explanation.definitionFit: Nantes is a large city in western France on the Loire, famous for its 1598 Edict.

clue.text: A couple of Scots cut off and shut off: no change here!

indicators.note: something off has gone wrong, so the word before it is jumbled

blocks.note: twa is Scots for two
to sever is to cut off
taken as written for the anagram

explanation.surface: Two Scotsmen are isolated and shut out, and nothing ever seems to change for them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut off and shut off' looks like a matched pair, but the first is a synonym and the second an anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying expresses resigned acceptance that things have always been like this and nothing alters.

clue.text: Hold our Peter's father, perhaps - one before 13

blocks.note: Peter Mandelson, the Labour politician, has a surname that jokingly reads as the son of this man
a nelson is a wrestling hold

explanation.surface: Someone asks us to keep hold of Peter's dad, apparently a figure who came before.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'perhaps' admits the joke: Mandelson is not really anybody's son. The two names sit in the grid surname first, at 25 then 24. The cross-reference points to Thabo Mbeki at 13 across.
explanation.definitionFit: Nelson Mandela was South Africa's president immediately before Thabo Mbeki took office in 1999.

clue.text: Where the flytrap was you can see little bits mangled inside

indicators.note: mangled things are crushed out of shape, so these letters lose their order
the jumbled bits go inside the small word

blocks.note: wee is Scottish for small
the letters of bits rearranged

explanation.surface: Visiting the spot where a Venus flytrap once grew, you find little scraps strewn about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flytrap' suggests the carnivorous plant, but here it is a spider's web, so a web site is where it was.
explanation.definitionFit: Read literally, a web site is the location of a spider's web, a trap for catching flies.
